## 1. What this is

A proposal to develop a healthcare-anchored building with medical retail at the street, flexible clinical and medical-office space above, structured parking, and mobility infrastructure — on a 0.88-acre corner in Fort Lauderdale's hospital corridor.

It is **proposed**, not approved. The sponsor does not currently own the property; this is a **prospective acquisition**. No entitlement, utility commitment, partner agreement, or financing exists.

This document does something prospectuses usually do not: it states where the project does not presently work. That is deliberate. The analysis behind it is the asset; a narrative that outran it would be worth nothing to a lender, a health system, or the City.

## 2. The site

Verified facts, corroborated across an independent appraisal, a third-party feasibility study, and the project's own corrected-assumptions record:

| | |
|---|---|
| Land area | **38,207 SF (0.88 acre)**, three parcels under a single folio (50-42-15-01-0711) |
| Frontage | **275 ft** on South Andrews Avenue · **170 ft** on SW 9th Street — a true corner |
| North boundary | **Florence C. Hardy Park** — open space no future neighbour can build out |
| Zoning | **RAC-RPO** (Regional Activity Center – Residential and Professional Office) |
| Flood | **FEMA Zone AE**, entire site, panel 12011C0557J (31 July 2024) |
| Existing | Three 1959-era one-storey commercial buildings, treated as interim use |
| Position | ~10 minutes' walk to downtown · 1.5 mi to I-95 · 1.8 mi to Brightline · 2.8 mi to Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International |
| Opportunity Zone | Federal QOZ designation — **source-derived and independently checkable; structuring advice not yet obtained** |

*Source: AEI appraisal (Sept 2025) pp. 3, 27–28, 37; Native Realty feasibility study (June 2026) pp. 1–3.*

## 3. Why healthcare

Broward Health's campus expansion sits adjacent to this corridor, and hospital consolidation reliably displaces independent and step-down practices that need nearby, flexible, well-parked space. Independent providers need what a hospital campus stops offering: smaller suites, shorter terms, easier parking, and a front door patients can find.

**This thesis is not yet validated.** The demand evidence in the project record cites a market study that is not in the repository, and the county's medical-office vacancy has been cited at 10.4%. No health system has been approached under any documented process, and none is committed. The appraisal — the most rigorous third-party document available — contains **no office rent, no medical-office rent, no office vacancy, and no office cap-rate data at all**; its market section is entirely retail.

What can be said: the location is right for the use, and the use is the most defensible one available for this parcel. What cannot be said: that demand at a given rent has been demonstrated.

## 4. What is proposed

Four scenarios were modelled. All areas and counts are **planning-level model outputs on a stated basis, subject to architectural test-fit** — not approved design.

| | Storeys | Total GSF | Clinical / office | Medical retail | Stalls | Development cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Minimum viable** | 4 | 108,000 | 20,400 RSF | 12,000 RSF | 169 | $40.9M core / $46.8M tenant-ready |
| **Balanced clinical + staging** | 6 | 160,000 | 40,800 RSF | 10,000 RSF | 231 | $59.9M core / $69.8M tenant-ready |
| **Maximum fleet** | 8 | 216,000 | 40,800 RSF | 10,000 RSF | 385 | $76.3M core / $86.3M tenant-ready |
| **Staging ground** | 1 | 14,000 | — | 14,000 RSF | 70 | $20.4M core |

All costs include the land input and are **AACE Class 5 planning estimates, accuracy −30% to +50%**, with no contractor pricing, no design documentation, no geotechnical report, and no utility study behind them.

**The recommended scheme is the four-storey minimum viable development** — not because it earns the most, but because it risks the least while preserving everything: it sits below the discretionary height-review threshold, parks itself with a modest surplus, needs only a conventional 480 V service, and is structured to grow vertically if the evidence later supports it.

## 5. What the numbers say

Presented without softening, because a reader who finds this later would rightly distrust anything else.

> **Both current financial models independently indicate that the base project, as presently modeled at the working land basis, does not satisfy the modeled institutional return requirements.**

Modelled yields on cost run 2.7%–4.1% against a 7.0% planning hurdle. And a residual analysis prepared for this document establishes something the earlier models did not test: **at a land basis of zero, no scenario exceeds a 4.49% yield on cost.** The shortfall is not a function of the acquisition price. It sits in the relationship between South Florida construction cost and the rents this program can plausibly command.

The office rent required to reach a 7.0% yield on the leading scheme is approximately **$131 per rentable square foot**. The modelled rent is $50, and the project's two models disagree about whether $36 or $50 is the right figure.

**What this means, precisely:** the project as currently configured is not investable on real-estate economics alone. It becomes investable only with a healthcare anchor, public capital, or a transaction structure that removes the fixed land obligation. That is the conversation this document exists to open — not a claim that the conversation has already succeeded.

## 6. Mobility, stated accurately

Structured parking, EV charging and vehicle staging are **enabling infrastructure and optionality**, not the business. No autonomous-vehicle, fleet, or charging revenue appears in any base case. No mobility operator has any relationship with this project; the operators active in the region are relevant context and nothing more.

Two findings are worth stating plainly because they cut against the project's own earlier hypotheses:

**Gross stalls are not fleet capacity.** After the building's own code-required parking, secure-zone boundary loss, turnaround and manoeuvring reserve, the eight-storey maximum-fleet scheme yields roughly **140 operational fleet positions — not the 300–400 originally contemplated.** Housing a vehicle in a structured deck on this land costs approximately **$545,000 per usable position.**

**That is why the operating model splits across two sites.** South Andrews becomes a high-throughput, low-storage transfer point: passenger pickup and drop-off, hospital staging, dispatch, 40 managed Level 2 chargers, clinical parking. Overnight storage, bulk charging, cleaning and maintenance move to a lower-cost industrial depot. That split reduces the required electrical service from roughly **3,208 kW to 1,143 kW** — from medium-voltage primary service to a conventional 480 V secondary — worth on the order of **$3M in avoided capital**.

**No depot site has been identified, priced, or secured.** Until one is, no mobility-specific infrastructure beyond chargers and the passenger-transfer canopy should be built.

## 7. Why this use rather than the alternatives

Comparison, not assertion.

| Alternative | Why it is not preferred |
|---|---|
| **Grocery or conventional retail** | Physically fits and is cheap to build, but forecloses the healthcare thesis permanently. On the appraisal's own data the retail market is softening: −510,000 SF net absorption over twelve months, rent growth down from 10.2% to 1.5% |
| **Bare parking garage** | **Not permittable.** A standalone commercial garage is not an enumerated principal use in RAC-RPO. It also has the worst economics tested — structured parking returns roughly 2–3% on fully loaded cost |
| **Pure fleet depot** | Same permitting problem, plus it puts industrial functions on the most expensive land in the programme at $545,000 per usable fleet position |
| **Generic medical office** | Self-defeating: more office demands more parking, and parking is the value-destroying component. The office-heavy stacks tested fall to 2.2 stalls per 1,000 RSF and fail their own parking test |
| **Residential** | The district permits **50 dwelling units per net acre — about 43 units.** This is not a tower site. The appraisal's two highest comparables were downtown RAC-CC sites carrying 381 and 316 units; that density is unavailable here. *Unless the Live Local Act preempts the cap — unverified, and the single highest-value unexplored question* |
| **Hotel / extended stay** | A permitted use that pairs naturally with airport and Brightline demand, but operator-dependent, cyclical, and it abandons the healthcare anchor without solving the parking cost |
| **Sell the land / do not acquire** | A serious option, honestly held. If the diligence below does not change the answer, this is the disciplined outcome |

The healthcare-anchored scheme wins on entitlement defensibility, civic contribution, and long-term adaptability. **It does not currently win on return, and this document does not claim it does.**

## 8. Approval pathway

No entitlement exists. The sequence is a **pre-application meeting with the City, a Zoning Verification Letter, land-use counsel opinion, architectural test-fit, traffic and stormwater engineering, then site-plan review.**

An honest reading of the record: heights above six floors "shall be reviewed" under the applicable provisions — a **discretionary, design-driven approval, not a by-right permit**. The controlling text in the appraisal is truncated mid-sentence in the source document, and the specific review level cited elsewhere appears in only one buy-side study with no ordinance text quoted. **The recommended four-storey scheme avoids the height-review trigger altogether.** That is a substantial part of why it is recommended.

The City will expect an active ground floor rather than a blank garage wall, a parking and use structure that fits the code, flood-resilient design, and a traffic and circulation solution. The proposal is built around those expectations: medical retail lines South Andrews, vehicle access is pushed to the secondary edges, and the frontage is never the fleet throat.

## 9. Public and economic benefit

Stated without quantification, because no economic-impact analysis exists and inventing one would be worse than saying so:

- Healthcare access on a transit-served corridor, complementing rather than competing with hospital expansion
- An activated, walkable street frontage replacing three vacant-facing 1959-era structures
- Flood-resilient design and stormwater capacity on a site entirely within Zone AE
- Publicly available EV charging
- A transfer point that reduces private-vehicle trips to the hospital campus
- Construction and permanent employment

## 10. What must happen next

A bounded pre-acquisition diligence programme of roughly **$100,000–$200,000**, all of which can be completed before any land commitment:

1. **Recover the existing Phase I and Phase II environmental reports.** Both are referenced by the appraisal; neither is in the project record. A Phase II is normally commissioned only after a Phase I identifies a condition. *Cheapest item, fastest, and capable of stopping the transaction.*
2. **FPL preliminary load letter.** A single budget line currently spans $750K–$5.0M.
3. **Land-use counsel opinion and City pre-application** — height pathway, parking method, accessory-parking limits, Live Local applicability.
4. **Architectural and parking test-fit** to fix the program basis.
5. **Medical-office rent comparables and absorption.**
6. **Contractor pricing** on two schemes.

Then, and only then, a decision on whether and how to acquire.

## 11. What is being sought

Not capital for a project that does not yet clear its hurdle. What would change the answer:

- **A healthcare anchor** — a master lease, minimum-use guarantee, or capital contribution worth roughly $1.6M–$2.3M per year of incremental income. This is the single most powerful lever available.
- **Public participation** — mobility-hub grants, TIF, or P3 structures covering $15M–$20M of development cost.
- **A transaction structure** — ground lease, option, seller participation, or land contribution — that converts a fixed land obligation into a variable one.
